title: Academic Writing
tagline: What research is, choosing a topic, finding literature, reading and notes, the literature review, structure and argument, citation and references, academic integrity, the language of scholarship, and the thesis and its defence
summary: A thesis in Chinese language or literature asks a question that has not yet been answered, places it among earlier work and answers it with evidence. This course covers choosing a topic, searching databases such as CNKI, reading and taking notes, writing a literature review, structuring the argument of a paper, citing according to the national standard, academic integrity, the language of scholarship, and writing and defending a graduation thesis.
overview: This course is about writing that other people can check. That single requirement explains almost all of its customs: the citation, the definition, the concession, the limitations section, the dull prose. A claim that can be verified by a stranger is the basic unit of scholarship, and everything else is scaffolding.

We start with what counts as a research question - one that could be answered differently, and for which someone could name the material that would settle it. Then the machinery: searching, reading, note-taking as an auditable practice, and the literature review, which is not a summary of what has been said but a map of what has been agreed, disputed, and left unasked.

Half the course is structure and language: how a scholarly paragraph is built, how to hedge proportionally to your evidence, how to concede without losing the point, and how to write a limitations section that is neither an apology nor a concealment.

The last chapters are about the rules that carry sanctions: citation systems, the taxonomies of misconduct, the difference between carelessness and fabrication, and the defence - the oral exam in which your written argument has to survive being questioned by someone who has read it.
outcomes: State a research question that is answerable, falsifiable in practice, and small enough for the material you can actually reach.
Search systematically: choose databases and keywords, record what you searched and what you excluded, and keep a reproducible trail.
Take notes in a form that lets a stranger audit your claims a year later.
Write a literature review organised by argument rather than by author, and end it with the gap your work addresses.
Structure an article so that each section performs one function, and build paragraphs as claim, warrant, evidence, qualification.
Use hedging proportional to evidence, and distinguish what your material shows from what you infer.
Apply a citation standard, explain the categories of misconduct, and defend a thesis orally against objections you did not anticipate.

chapters.summary: Libraries, CNKI and other databases, databases of classical texts, and keeping track of sources.

chapters.summary: Reading scholarship critically, and notes that keep quotation, paraphrase and one’s own ideas apart.

chapters.title: The literature review
chapters.summary: Synthesising earlier work by question rather than by author, and finding the gap.

chapters.title: Structure and argument
chapters.summary: Introduction, body and conclusion, primary texts as evidence, and close reading in an argument.

chapters.summary: Direct and indirect quotation, footnotes, and the national standard for references, GB/T 7714—2015.

chapters.title: Academic integrity
chapters.summary: Plagiarism, self-plagiarism and fabrication, similarity checking, and using AI tools within the rules.

chapters.title: The language of scholarship

chapters.title: The thesis and its defence
chapters.summary: Planning and writing a graduation thesis, working with a supervisor, and the oral defence.

history.title: An inventory of argument
history.detail: A Greek treatise sorts the kinds of reasoning, the places where arguments come from, and the emotions a speaker may use - the first lasting vocabulary for justifying a claim.

history.title: The disputed question
history.detail: Medieval schools develop a fixed procedure for handling an open question: state the question, list objections, answer, reply to each objection; students still learn its shape without knowing its origin.

history.title: A forgery proved by language
history.detail: A scholar shows that a celebrated charter must be late, using the anachronisms of its Latin; philology becomes a tool of evidence rather than of erudition.

history.title: Against the idols of the mind
history.detail: A philosophical work argues that inquiry must begin by cataloguing its own biases, and proposes induction from particulars as the alternative to syllogism.

history.title: The journal
history.detail: The first periodicals for the publication of inquiries appear; priority, brevity and a dated record become properties of research.

history.title: The seminar
history.detail: A new university model joins research and teaching; students are trained by working on open problems under supervision, and the thesis becomes the credential.

history.title: Go and find the material
history.detail: A research institute is founded with a programme that treats newly excavated documents, field records and objects as equal in standing to transmitted texts.
history.people: Fu Sinian and the history-language institute

history.title: Against counting only
history.detail: Reform documents in several countries begin to restrict the use of publication counts and journal rankings as hiring criteria, after decades in which the metric became the objective.

references.title: How to Write a Thesis
references.author: Umberto Eco
references.note: Still the best account of the material crafts of scholarship: cards, files, and patience.

references.title: Writing for Social Scientists
references.author: Howard S. Becker
references.note: On writing anxiety as a social product; read before you draft your first article.

references.title: The Craft of Research
references.author: Wayne C. Booth and others
references.note: The claim-evidence-warrant frame in its most teachable form.

references.title: The Method of Chinese History
references.author: Liang Qichao
references.note: A foundational lecture course on evidence, error and the writing of history in modern China.

references.title: On the Investigation of Ancient Chinese History
references.author: Gu Jiegang (ed.)
references.note: A self-confessing preface that models how to show your reasoning and your doubts together.

references.title: The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons
references.author: Liu Xie
references.note: Noted here for one thing: the oldest sustained analysis in Chinese of how arguments are built.

references.title: Information and Documentation: Rules for Diplomas and Patents (GB/T 7714)
references.author: Standardisation Administration
references.note: The national citation standard you will be required to follow; learn its two systems, not all of its examples.
